 Changes come to Pell Grant, student loan eligibility: What Nicholls students need to know ahead of spring advising
 Julianne Neigel , Editor-in-Chief 
 • 
 October 21, 2026 
 Photo by: Emilee Theriot Otto B. Candies Hall, Nicholls State University. 
 Jackson Moreaux, KNSU TV
 Nicholls Financial Aid 
 The U.S. Department of Education announced changes to 2026-2027 Pell Grant and student loan policies following the implementation of President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” in July 2025, potentially impacting part-time and course-withdrawing students. 
 The bill established lifetime caps on undergraduate loans and changed eligibility requirements for Pell Grants for the 2026-2027 academic year, according to the revised Federal Student Aid Handbook .  
 Students now have to be enrolled in at least six hours, or in half-time status, to be eligible for a Federal Direct Loan. According to Nicholls’ fall enrollment statistics, 53% of students have received a federal loan. 
 Changes also included adjustments to the percentage of a Pell Grant a student qualifies for. Students who enroll less than 12 hours, or below full-time status, may now be eligible for a reduced Pell Grant award.  
 Students now receive awards based on their schedule’s enrollment intensity, or the percentage resulting from dividing their scheduled hours by standard full-time enrollment hours. For example, a student enrolling in seven credit hours will now qualify for 58% of their Pell Grant award. 
 Dropping or failing a course, or simply enrolling in fewer hours, may significantly impact a student’s financial aid eligibility for future semesters as a result.  
 Nicholls calculates the cost of an academic year by doubling a student’s fall semester course load. This means any changes in hours may result in having to make up hours in the spring. 
 “The biggest issue with this change to students is when a student drops a class or ends up failing a class. Because if you fail a class, you earn zero hours,” said Brandy St. Pierre, Nicholls’ associate director of financial aid and scholarships.  
 “That will also require a change for the spring semester because they didn’t earn those hours.” 
 “Assuming they’ve attended classes, they’re not going to owe anything for this semester when they drop. However, with this new change, we will now be adjusting their spring loans, so that student would need to be enrolled in at least nine hours for the spring to make up what we would have adjusted,” St. Pierre said. 
 This policy does not apply to graduating students who are enrolled half-time. These students will undergo proration, or the adjustment of their financial aid and cost of attendance. 
 Non-graduating students who are not enrolled full-time—such as culinary, education or nursing students taking partial-credit laboratory classes, for example—do not undergo this process. Enrollment intensity may affect these students more. 
 “Because [graduating students] are running through proration, it’s handled a little differently than a student who is not full-time, like our nursing students.” St. Pierre said. 
 “If they’re in clinicals, they may only be in seven hours that semester. They’re not graduating, so they’re not prorated. They’re looked at with enrollment intensity and through the schedule of reduction. So that might affect those students, like it can affect culinary [and] education [students].” 
 Students are urged to consider future semesters and consult their degree plans ahead of advising, as they may have to adjust their schedules to be eligible for their full award amount each semester. 
 “You can take 15 and 15 [credit hours], and continue down where you’re full-time each term, and that way you’re getting the most beneficial amount of all your financial aid, grant money, loan money, TOPs, academic scholarships,” St. Pierre said. 
 “Because if you’re not full-time, all of that is basically being adjusted. With advising going on now, work with your adviser on what you can take to try to remain full-time until you graduate.” 
 Any student considering withdrawing from a course is advised to consult Financial Aid. While other options may be available, the withdrawing process cannot be reversed once paperwork has begun. 
 “Come talk to Financial Aid before any sort of paperwork is done, so we can go through the ramifications of all of that. Even [with] dropping, you wouldn’t want to lose eligibility for other forms of financial aid that you’re receiving if you drop without coming talk to us first,” St. Pierre said. 
 “We can work through scenarios, but once you start the paperwork to drop or resign that process has begun, so you gotta kind of finish the process. Always come talk to Financial Aid or Scholarships.” 
 Nicholls’ Department of Financial Aid is located in Otto B. Candies Hall. The office can be reached by email at [email protected] , or by phone at 985-448-4048.
